name: The Excretory System
what: Covers the removal of nitrogenous waste and the maintenance of water balance in mammals, including the structure and function of the kidney, the nephron filtration process, and the malfunctions of UTIs and kidney disease.
why: The excretory system demonstrates specialised cells forming functional units (nephrons) within organs, and provides a concrete context for osmosis, active transport and hormonal regulation that recurs in Units 3 and 4.

items.title: I can explain the origin of nitrogenous waste and why it must be excreted
items.what: Excess amino acids cannot be stored and are broken down by deamination in the liver. This releases the amine group, which is converted to toxic ammonia and then to less toxic urea for excretion in urine.
items.why: Understanding why nitrogenous waste forms and why different organisms excrete different forms (ammonia, urea, uric acid) is a study design requirement that connects metabolism to excretion.
items.example: A fish living in water excretes ammonia directly across its gills because water is abundant. Humans convert ammonia to urea in the liver because urea is far less toxic and requires less water to excrete — an adaptation for terrestrial life.

items.title: I can identify the structures of the mammalian excretory system and describe the role of each
items.what: The system includes two kidneys (filter blood), two ureters (carry urine to the bladder), the bladder (stores urine) and the urethra (expels urine). The renal artery delivers blood and the renal vein returns filtered blood.
items.why: Structural identification of excretory organs is directly tested and provides the spatial context needed to explain filtration and reabsorption processes.
items.example: Each kidney receives oxygenated blood via the renal artery, filters approximately 180 litres of plasma per day, and returns cleaned blood via the renal vein — only about 1.8 litres of urine is actually excreted.

items.title: I can describe the nephron as the functional unit of the kidney and identify its key structural regions
items.what: The nephron consists of the Bowman's capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle (descending and ascending), distal tubule and collecting duct. It is closely associated with the glomerulus and peritubular capillaries.
items.why: The nephron is the site of filtration, reabsorption and secretion and is the focus of the most complex excretory system exam questions, including those linking osmosis and active transport to specific tubule regions.
items.example: Each human kidney contains approximately 0.8–1.5 million nephrons. If all nephrons from both kidneys were laid end to end, the total tubule length would be approximately 80 km.

items.title: I can explain filtration, reabsorption and secretion in the nephron and where each occurs
items.what: Filtration: blood pressure forces water and small solutes from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule (proteins are excluded). Reabsorption: useful substances and water move from the tubule back into peritubular capillaries. Secretion: additional waste solutes are actively transported from blood into the tubule.
items.why: These three processes define how the nephron converts blood plasma into urine and are the basis for all quantitative questions about changes in filtrate composition along the nephron.
items.example: By the end of the proximal tubule, 65% of filtered water and ions, and 100% of filtered glucose and amino acids, have been reabsorbed. By the collecting duct, 99% of filtrate has been reclaimed, leaving approximately 1.8 L of urine per day.

items.title: I can trace the change in filtrate composition from the Bowman's capsule to the collecting duct
items.what: Filtrate in the Bowman's capsule contains water, glucose, amino acids, ions and urea (no proteins). As it progresses, glucose and amino acids are fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, water is continuously reabsorbed, and urea becomes increasingly concentrated, representing 2% of urine compared to 0.03% in blood plasma.
items.why: Tracing composition changes is a standard exam task and requires integrating knowledge of osmosis, active transport and ADH regulation in a single coherent sequence.
items.example: A patient with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes will have glucose present in their urine, because blood glucose is so elevated that the proximal tubule transport proteins become saturated and cannot reabsorb all filtered glucose.

items.title: I can explain the role of ADH in regulating water reabsorption and how this connects the excretory and endocrine systems
items.what: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) is released from the posterior pituitary when blood osmolality rises (e.g. during dehydration). It increases the water permeability of the distal tubule and collecting duct, allowing more water to be reabsorbed by osmosis.
items.why: ADH action is a key cross-system example linking the endocrine and excretory systems, and it is a model for how negative feedback maintains water homeostasis.
items.example: After running 10 km without drinking, blood solute concentration rises above the normal range. The posterior pituitary releases more ADH, the collecting duct becomes more permeable to water, urine volume decreases and becomes more concentrated — often darker yellow in colour.

items.title: I can describe the cause, symptoms and consequences of UTIs and kidney disease
items.what: UTIs are bacterial infections (typically E. coli) of the urethra or bladder, more common in females due to the shorter urethra (4 cm vs 20 cm in males). Chronic kidney disease involves progressive loss of nephron function and can require dialysis or transplant.
items.why: Excretory system malfunctions are study design requirements and test whether students can apply structural and functional knowledge to pathological contexts.
items.example: Chronic kidney disease can progress to 90% loss of nephron function before symptoms appear, because the remaining nephrons hypertrophy and compensate. Once symptoms such as high blood pressure and oedema emerge, significant irreversible damage has usually already occurred.
